items.title: Al Gallodoro Interview, 1966-05-10
items.q: But when I got to Atlantic City, George Olsen had left the night before. So I was more or less stuck.

ctx.x: This was the one Sal Franzella used to talk about. Instead of talking about anyone, he would always talk about your ability as a saxophonist and clarinet. Is that the one he had great admiration for your performance and playing? Adrian Fresh?

Adrian Fresh? Possibly. He's probably deceased now. But when I got to Atlantic City, George Olsen had left the night before. So I was more or less stuck. But I saw that next door to the hotel that Olsen was in, Isham Jones. I-A-I-S-H-A-M. Isham Jones. He was some composer. He was a multi-millionaire when he passed away at Turkey Ranch. He wrote all of those beautiful tunes like Swinging Down the Lane and things like that. Anyway, I went to see his manager and he was interested in what I had to say. He gave me an…
What are they planning on putting there? Are they planning on building Newwood?

items.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005
items.q: He said, “He’s playing with George Olsen.” George Olsen was a big name at this time.

ctx.x: And did have you have a specific destination?

Yeah. New York. But I had to stop in Philadelphia first, because Danny Ryan, who was a trumpet player that I played with in a nightclub, he wanted me to go to New York with him. I says, “Danny, I’m not ready yet.” But then when finally the theater closed, the Orpheum Theater closed, that’s when I headed for New York, but I stopped in Philadelphia. I stopped in Philadelphia, this is good. I stopped at the rooming house and the lady came out, she says, “Oh Danny is not here, he is playing in Ocean City with Ray”…

great singer. He is at the Ritz Carlton. Don’t ask me how I got to Atlantic City from Ocean City, I must have taken a bus. I think what did we do, only 20 years old, we had no fear. And he was gone. George Olsen had gone. But at the Ambassador Hotel I see Isham Jones, oh my God, Isham Jones was a big name at that time. “It Had to be You,” “I’ll See You in my Dreams.” And the story is the same. I went to the dining room and to the maitre d’ I says, “Is it possible to see Mr. Jones?” He says, “Oh no, no, no, you…
